content: Cannabidiol, commonly referred to as CBD, is a non-intoxicating cannabinoid derived from the hemp plant, Cannabis sativa. It is one of the primary components of the plant, comprising up to 40% of its extracts. While CBD itself does not produce intoxicating effects, it appears to modulate the euphoric effects of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), which is an isomer of cannabidiol. Additionally, CBD may impart a sedative effect. However, some studies suggest that CBD can also enhance alertness. It has been observed that CBD may slow the clearance of THC from the body, potentially by interfering with THC metabolism in the liver. Unlike THC, CBD does not seem to directly interact with the CB1 or CB2 cannabinoid receptors. From a medical perspective, CBD has demonstrated potential therapeutic effects, including the ability to alleviate convulsions, reduce inflammation, mitigate anxiety, and relieve nausea. Furthermore, it has shown promise in inhibiting the growth of cancer cells. Recent research has indicated that CBD may be as effective as atypical antipsychotic medications in the treatment of schizophrenia. In April 2005, Canadian health authorities approved the use of Sativex, an oromucosal spray designed to alleviate pain associated with multiple sclerosis. Sativex contains both THC and CBD and is marketed in Canada by GW Pharmaceuticals. Beyond its use in multiple sclerosis, CBD has also been found to inhibit the growth of cancer cells while exhibiting low toxicity in non-cancerous cells. Although the precise mechanisms underlying this effect are not yet fully understood, research by Ligresti et al. suggests that CBD exerts its anticancer effects through a combination of mechanisms. These include direct or indirect activation of CB2 and TRPV1 receptors, induction of oxidative stress, and promotion of apoptosis (programmed cell death) in cancer cells.
